questions.text: Sovereignty is best defined as the
options: supreme and absolute power of the state
questions.explanation: Sovereignty is the supreme, absolute and permanent power of the state over its territory, with no higher authority above it.

questions.text: Legitimacy differs from power in that legitimacy refers to
options: the control of the armed forces
the acceptance of authority by the governed
questions.explanation: Legitimacy is the recognised right to rule, accepted by the people. Power is the mere ability to compel obedience, with or without acceptance.

questions.text: A nation differs from a state in that a nation is
options: always independent, while a state is not
a people bound by common identity, while a state is a politically organised community with sovereignty
a larger political unit than a state
questions.explanation: A nation is defined by shared culture, history or identity; a state adds territory, government and sovereignty. A nation may exist without a state of its own.

questions.text: Political socialisation is the process by which citizens
options: acquire political values, beliefs and attitudes
questions.explanation: Through family, school, peers and the media, individuals learn the political culture of their society. Voting, joining parties and contesting are forms of participation.

questions.text: Authority differs from power because authority is
options: power that is recognised as legitimate
questions.explanation: Authority is institutionalised, legitimate power that people accept as rightful. Raw power may rest on force or wealth without legitimacy.

questions.text: The term 'state' in political science refers to
options: a group of people with common ancestry
a politically organised community with a definite territory, population, government and sovereignty
questions.explanation: A state combines people, territory, government and sovereignty. A province is a sub-unit of a federation, and a government is only the machinery that runs the state.

questions.text: A system of government in which power is held by a small group of wealthy or privileged people is known as
questions.explanation: Oligarchy is rule by a few. Democracy is rule by the people, monarchy is rule by a king or queen, and theocracy is rule by religious leaders.

questions.text: In a federal system of government, residual powers are exercised by the
questions.explanation: Residual powers — matters not listed in the constitution — belong to the states in a federation such as Nigeria. Exclusive powers belong to the centre.

questions.text: Rule by religious leaders in the name of a deity is known as
questions.explanation: Theocracy is government by religious leaders claiming divine authority. Aristocracy is rule by nobles, autocracy by one absolute ruler, and republicanism by elected representatives.

questions.text: A confederal system of government is one in which
options: the central government can override the states at will
sovereign states retain most powers and delegate only a few to a central body
all powers are held by the central government
powers are shared equally between centre and regions
questions.explanation: In a confederation the component states are sovereign and the centre is weak, e.g. the former Senegambia. A unitary system concentrates power at the centre.

questions.text: In a presidential system of government, the president
options: is a ceremonial head of state only
can be removed by a vote of no confidence
is both head of state and head of government
questions.explanation: Nigeria's president combines both roles and is elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term, unlike a prime minister who depends on legislative confidence.

questions.text: A republic is a state in which
options: the head of state is elected and not a hereditary monarch
questions.explanation: In a republic, sovereignty resides in the people and the head of state is chosen, usually by election, rather than inheriting the office.

questions.text: The primary function of the legislature in a democratic state is to
questions.explanation: The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them, and the judiciary interprets them.

questions.text: In a parliamentary system of government, the head of government is the
questions.explanation: The prime minister, drawn from the legislature, heads the government in a parliamentary system. A president heads the government in a presidential system.

questions.text: The independence of the judiciary is best guaranteed by
options: security of tenure and adequate remuneration of judges
appointment of judges by the president
control of the courts by the legislature
election of judges by the people
questions.explanation: Judges who cannot be removed arbitrarily and are well paid can decide cases without fear or favour. Executive control over the courts undermines independence.

questions.text: The political ideology that advocates collective ownership of the means of production is
questions.explanation: Socialism places major means of production under public or collective ownership. Capitalism favours private ownership, feudalism is based on land and lordship, and fascism on extreme nationalism and dictatorship.

questions.text: Which of the following is a source of a constitution?
questions.explanation: Court decisions interpreting the law form part of constitutional sources, along with statutes, conventions and customs. Party constitutions and editorials are not sources of the national constitution.

questions.text: The Nigerian National Assembly consists of the Senate and the
questions.explanation: The National Assembly is bicameral: the Senate with 109 members and the House of Representatives with 360 members.

questions.text: The Clifford Constitution of 1922 is notable because it introduced
questions.explanation: The Clifford Constitution allowed the election of four members to the Legislative Council — three for Lagos and one for Calabar — the first elections in Nigeria.

questions.text: The Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 is significant because it
options: established a true federal system in Nigeria
questions.explanation: The 1954 Constitution made Nigeria a federation, with regional governments exercising residual powers and Lagos as a federal territory. Independence came in 1960.

questions.text: The Richards Constitution of 1946 was criticised mainly because it
questions.explanation: The Richards Constitution was drawn up in London with little Nigerian input, though it did introduce regional councils. It did not introduce federalism or independence.

questions.text: Nigeria became a republic in
questions.explanation: The 1963 Republican Constitution replaced the Queen with a Nigerian president as head of state. Independence was in 1960 and the first military coup in 1966.

questions.text: The doctrine of separation of powers is best associated with
questions.explanation: Montesquieu's 'The Spirit of the Laws' (1748) argued for separating legislative, executive and judicial powers to prevent tyranny.

questions.text: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 introduced
options: regional legislatures and a central Council of Ministers
questions.explanation: The 1951 Constitution created regional Houses of Assembly and a Council of Ministers at the centre, but retained a unitary framework; true federalism came in 1954.

questions.text: The pre-colonial Igbo political system is best described as
options: acephalous, with authority shared by village assemblies and age grades
highly centralised under a single king
questions.explanation: Igbo society had no single centralised ruler; decisions were taken by the village assembly, council of elders, age grades and title holders.

questions.text: The first military coup in Nigeria took place in
questions.explanation: The January 1966 coup led by Major Nzeogwu ended the First Republic. Later coups occurred in 1975, 1983, 1985 and 1993.

questions.text: In the pre-colonial Yoruba political system, the body that could check the powers of the Alaafin of Oyo was the
questions.explanation: The Oyomesi, a council of seven chiefs led by the Bashorun, could reject the Alaafin's decisions and order his suicide, providing a real check on his power.

questions.text: The principle that 13% of oil revenue should go directly to oil-producing states is known as
questions.explanation: The derivation principle, in the 1999 Constitution, returns 13% of revenue from natural resources to the states where they are derived.

questions.text: The 1979 Constitution of Nigeria introduced
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution replaced the parliamentary system with an American-style executive presidency, an executive president and the federal character principle.

questions.text: Under the 1999 Constitution, matters on the Exclusive Legislative List can be legislated upon only by the
questions.explanation: The Exclusive List — defence, currency, aviation, customs — is reserved to the federal legislature. State assemblies legislate on residual matters and share the Concurrent List.

questions.text: The principle that no person is above the law and that all are equal before the law is known as
questions.explanation: The rule of law means laws apply equally to rulers and ruled. Separation of powers divides government functions, and federal character concerns fair representation.

questions.text: A Nigerian citizen by birth can acquire the citizenship of another country without losing Nigerian citizenship because the 1999 Constitution permits
options: dual citizenship for citizens by birth
questions.explanation: Section 28 of the 1999 Constitution allows a Nigerian by birth to hold dual citizenship; a citizen by registration or naturalisation who takes another citizenship forfeits Nigerian citizenship.

questions.text: A constitution that can only be amended through a special and difficult procedure is described as
questions.explanation: A rigid constitution requires special majorities or procedures for amendment, as with Nigeria's 1999 Constitution. A flexible constitution is amended like ordinary law.

questions.text: The 1976 local government reform in Nigeria is significant because it
options: gave local governments control of the police
created a uniform system of local government throughout the federation
questions.explanation: The 1976 reform standardised local government structure, functions and funding nationwide, recognising local government as a third tier of government.

questions.text: The annulment of the 12 June 1993 presidential election, believed to have been won by Moshood Abiola, was carried out by the regime of
questions.explanation: The Babangida regime annulled the 12 June 1993 election. Abacha later detained Abiola, and Abdulsalami conducted the transition to the Fourth Republic in 1999.

questions.text: The creation of twelve states in Nigeria in 1967 was carried out by the regime of
questions.explanation: Gowon replaced the four regions with twelve states in May 1967, on the eve of the civil war. Murtala created seven more states in 1976.

questions.text: The minimum voting age in Nigeria is
questions.explanation: Under the 1999 Constitution and the Electoral Act, every Nigerian citizen aged 18 and above is entitled to register and vote.

questions.text: The electoral system in which the candidate with the highest number of votes wins, even without an absolute majority, is the
questions.explanation: First-past-the-post, used in Nigeria's legislative elections, awards the seat to the plurality winner. Proportional representation allocates seats by vote share.

questions.text: Laws made by a body other than the legislature under powers delegated to it by the legislature are called
questions.explanation: Delegated legislation includes regulations, orders and rules made by ministers or agencies under an enabling Act. Decrees are military laws and edicts are state military laws.

questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic of the civil service?
questions.explanation: Civil servants remain in office despite changes of government, giving continuity. They are expected to be neutral, anonymous and expert, not partisan or profit-seeking.

questions.text: Citizenship by naturalisation in Nigeria requires, among other conditions, that the applicant must have
options: resided in Nigeria for a continuous period of fifteen years
questions.explanation: Under the 1999 Constitution, naturalisation requires fifteen years' continuous residence, good character, and willingness to renounce other citizenship and take an oath of allegiance.

questions.text: The principle of checks and balances ensures that
options: each arm of government can limit the powers of the others
power is concentrated in one arm
questions.explanation: Checks and balances let each arm restrain the others — e.g. the legislature approves budgets and the courts can declare laws unconstitutional.

questions.text: The first political party in Nigeria was the
options: National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC)
questions.explanation: The NNDP was founded by Herbert Macaulay in 1923, following the elective principle. The NCNC came in 1944, and the AG and NPC in 1951.

questions.text: The Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) is best classified as
questions.explanation: The NLC presses government on workers' interests without seeking political office itself, which is the defining feature of a pressure group.

questions.text: A one-party system is characterised by
options: only one political party being legally permitted to operate
questions.explanation: In a one-party system a single party is legally allowed, as in some post-independence African states. Two dominant parties make a two-party system.

questions.text: The body responsible for conducting elections into federal and state offices in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: INEC, established in 1998, conducts elections, registers voters and political parties, and delimits constituencies.

questions.text: The body that registered voters and conducted the 1979 general elections in Nigeria was the
questions.explanation: FEDECO ran the 1979 transition elections. INEC, created in 1998, runs elections in the Fourth Republic.

questions.text: For a candidate to win the Nigerian presidential election at the first ballot, the candidate must secure the highest number of votes and at least 25% of the votes in
options: two-thirds of the states and the Federal Capital Territory
questions.explanation: Section 134 of the 1999 Constitution requires the spread of 25% in at least two-thirds of the states and the FCT, ensuring broad national support.

questions.text: The headquarters of the African Union is situated in
questions.explanation: The African Union, successor to the OAU in 2002, has its headquarters in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. ECOWAS is headquartered in Abuja.

questions.text: The United Nations was founded in
questions.explanation: The UN was established in 1945 after the Second World War, replacing the League of Nations founded in 1919.

questions.text: ECOWAS was established by the Treaty of Lagos in
questions.explanation: The Economic Community of West African States was founded in 1975 to promote economic integration in West Africa.

questions.text: The headquarters of OPEC is located in
questions.explanation: OPEC's secretariat is in Vienna, Austria. The UN headquarters is in New York and the Commonwealth secretariat in London.

questions.text: The five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council are the USA, UK, France, Russia and
questions.explanation: The five permanent members, each holding the veto, are the USA, UK, France, Russia and China.

questions.text: The Commonwealth of Nations is headed by the
questions.explanation: The British monarch is the symbolic Head of the Commonwealth, a voluntary association of 56 states, most of them former British territories.

questions.text: The main focus of Nigeria's foreign policy since independence has been
questions.explanation: Nigeria's foreign policy has consistently placed Africa at its centre, supporting decolonisation, African unity and regional integration.

questions.text: Nigeria's membership of OPEC dates back to
questions.explanation: Nigeria joined the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries in 1971, eleven years after OPEC's founding in 1960.

questions.text: The principle of non-alignment in foreign policy means that a country
options: does not formally align with any major power bloc
questions.explanation: Non-alignment means independence of judgement in world affairs rather than loyalty to a bloc; Nigeria practised it while joining the UN, AU and Commonwealth.

questions.text: Nigeria's foreign policy objectives are stated in the 1999 Constitution under the
options: Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy
questions.explanation: Section 19, in Chapter II of the 1999 Constitution, sets out foreign policy objectives including African unity, non-alignment and world peace.

questions.text: The ECOMOG military intervention force was established by
questions.explanation: ECOMOG, the ECOWAS Monitoring Group, intervened in Liberia and Sierra Leone in the 1990s to restore peace.

questions.text: Nigeria's Afrocentric foreign policy was most clearly demonstrated by its leading role in
options: the liberation struggle in Southern Africa
questions.explanation: Nigeria championed decolonisation and the anti-apartheid struggle, including the nationalisation of British Petroleum's Nigerian interests in 1979 and support for frontline states.
